examples.subject: special issue jetai
examples.body: call for papers journal of experimental and theoretical artificial intelligence special issue on memory-based language processing memory - based language processing ( mblp ) views language processing as being based on the direct reuse of previous experience rather than on the use of abstractions extracted from that experience . in such a framework , language acquisition is modeled as the storage of exemplars , and language processing as similarity-based reasoning . mblp derives from work in artificial intelligence ( case-based reasoning , memory-based reasoning , instance-based learning , lazy learning ) , linguistics ( analogical modeling ) , computational linguistics ( example-based machine translation , case-based language processing , data-oriented parsing ) , and statistical pattern recognition ( k-nn models ) . in recent research , it has been shown that the application of algorithms based on this framework leads to accurate and efficient language models in diverse language processing areas ( phonology , morphology , syntax , semantics , discourse ) . we invite theoretical papers on models , algorithms and metrics for memory-based language processing , and empirical studies comparing mblp variants to each other or to alternative non-memory - based approaches for specific language processing tasks . time table deadline for submissions : september 1 , 1998 notification date : november 1 , 1998 deadline for final versions : january 1 , 1999 special issue : summer or autumn 1999 instructions for authors : 1 . the original manuscript and three clear copies should be submitted to : walter daelemans ( guest editor ) ilk research group , computational linguistics tilburg university warandelaan 2 5037 gc tilburg building b , room 307 the netherlands + 31 13 4663070 ( phone ) + 31 13 4663110 ( fax ) walter . daelemans @ kub . nl all papers will be refereed by at least three reviewers . 2 . all papers must be in english . the entire manuscript should be typed on one side only of plain paper , either a4 or 8 . 5 x 11 inch , with double spacing used throughout . 3 . the first page of the manuscript should carry the title , the names , institutional addresses , and institutional telephone numbers of the authors , and a short title of no more than 50 characters ( including spaces ) to be used as a running head . the second page of the manuscript should carry an abstract of about 200 words . the remainder of the text should not exceed 30 double spaced pages , including references but excluding figures and tables . all figures and tables must be referred to by number in the text . 4 . an original set of professional quality figures should accompany the manuscript . line drawing may be india ink originals or glossy prints . halftone illustrations must be submitted as glossy prints . illustrations cannot be printed in color . 5 . tables should be typed on separate pages , which should accompany the text . 6 . the text should be written in third person to facilitate blind reviewing . the names of the authors or their institutions should appear only on the title page . 7 . the name-date style should be used for all references . all authors ' names should be included in the reference list . journal names should not be abbreviated . inclusive page numbers must be given for all references to articles in journals , proceedings volumes , or books . with the exception of theses or dissertations , unpublished works should not be included as references . 8 . footnotes may not be used . endnotes may be used if necessary ; they should be collected on separate sheets at the end of the text . 9 . fifty free offprints will be provided to the first author of each paper . there will be no page charges .

examples.subject: Re: [SMB] NTCreateANDX quesiotn
examples.body:
On Mon, 11 Jun 2007 15:50:04 -0500
"Christopher R. Hertel"  wrote:

> > WordCount
> > 00000:  2a                                               |*               |
> > Words
> > 00000:  ff 00 87 00 03 00 c0 01 00 00 00 80 65 7a c2 f5  |............ez..|
> > 00010:  77 c3 01 5e 1b 3e 77 91 6c c6 01 80 65 7a c2 f5  |w..^.>w.l...ez..|
> > 00020:  77 c3 01 28 34 0f 62 2d 21 c4 01 20 00 00 00 00  |w..(4.b-!.. ....|
> > 00030:  f0 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 e8 00 00 00 00 00 00 00  |................|
> > 00040:  00 07 00 00 00 00 00 70 00 2e 00 65 00 78 00 65  |.......p...e.x.e|
> > 00050:  00 00 00 00                                      |....            |
> > Unknown
> > 00000:  00 03 81 d8 bf 03 81 20 ff 01 1f 00 00 00 00 00  |....... ........|
> > 00010:  00 00                                            |..              |
> > 
> > So I see 'p.exe' in the Words and Wireshark doesn't decode those bytes
> > so it looks like there's just garbage at the end. Meaning the WordCount
> > and the NetBIOS header payload size are incorrect (too large).
> 
> So... my next question.  Is the WordCount value 42 (0x2a) correct (for this
> packet)?  If so, then the "p.exe" string really is part of the Words.
> 
> ...but you said earlier that you thought the correct value should be closer
> to 34 (0x22).  If that were the case, the bytecount would be zero and
> 'p.exe' would not be part of the packet at all.
> 
> I am curious as to how this packet should be read.

How it "should" read is not important. What is important is the algorithm
by which you decode and encode this packet.

This packet's size is whatever the NetBIOS header says it is. There are
no Bytes in an SMB_COM_NT_CREATE_ANDX and therefore the WordCount should
just be ignored by clients and encoded by servers with the incorrect
value of 0x2a. Clients and servers should then decode / encode whatever
parts of the Words they know the format for. The remainder of the packet
should contain the user's horiscope or perhaps a fortune.

Mike

-- 
Michael B Allen

problem_definition.description: The data represents a cybersecurity threat scenario where malicious actors use email communications to deliver phishing and spam content. Malicious emails often contain promotional or urgent language in the subject and body, including offers for financial gain, health products, or fraudulent business opportunities. These emails embed suspicious URLs and use formatting tricks such as reply prefixes and mailing list tags to appear legitimate. The benign emails contrast with neutral or technical language, often containing conversational or informational content without promotional intent. The threat exploits user trust in email communications to induce clicks on malicious links or engagement with fraudulent offers.
problem_definition.asset_targeted: End Users (via deception to obtain sensitive information or induce action)

indicators_of_compromise: Subject lines with promotional or urgent language (e.g., 'Part-Time opportunity - $2000/week')
Presence of special characters, encoded content, and HTML-like tags in email bodies
Use of reply prefixes ('Re:'), mailing list tags (e.g., '[zzzzteana]') in subjects
Malicious emails often include calls to action or financial inducements
Sender/source labels associated with known malicious datasets (e.g., 'TREC-07', 'Enron')
attack_patterns: Use of persuasive language to lure recipients into clicking links or responding
Embedding URLs that lead to potentially harmful websites
Impersonation or spoofing tactics using familiar mailing list tags or reply formatting
Long, multi-paragraph email bodies with elaborate narratives to build trust
Inclusion of fake business or financial opportunity scenarios (e.g., inheritance scams)
normal_patterns: Neutral or technical language in subjects and bodies
Emails often structured as replies or discussions in mailing lists
Presence of legitimate email headers and formatting
Absence of promotional or urgent calls to action
Sources associated with benign datasets (e.g., 'Ling', 'TREC-07' with non-malicious content)

risk_reduction: Implement robust email filtering solutions that analyze subject and body content for promotional and suspicious language patterns
Deploy URL reputation and sandboxing technologies to detect and block malicious links
User awareness training to recognize phishing tactics and suspicious email characteristics
Use of sender authentication protocols such as SPF, DKIM, and DMARC to reduce spoofing
Monitor email source categories to identify and block high-risk origins
problem_definition.data_source_notes: The dataset contains well-structured email samples with clear labeling (malicious=1, benign=0) and preserved schema reflecting realistic email subject and body patterns. The presence of known data sources such as 'TREC-07' and 'Enron' enhances reliability. Label distribution and content correlations align with expected phishing and benign email characteristics, supporting strong confidence in the analysis.

value_patterns: Short to medium length text strings
Includes alphanumeric characters, punctuation, and special characters
Typical length ranges from a few words to about 10-15 words
May include email or group references in brackets

constraints.format_pattern: Free text with optional mailing list tags or reply prefixes

subject.generation_instructions: Generate varied text strings resembling email subjects, optionally including reply prefixes ('Re:'), mailing list tags in brackets (e.g., '[zzzzteana]'), and typical punctuation. Length should be roughly 5-15 words. Include alphanumeric and special characters as in real email subjects.
subject.relationship_to_label: Malicious subjects often contain promotional or urgent language (e.g., 'Guaranteed to lose 10-12 lbs', 'Life Insurance - Why Pay More?'), while benign subjects tend to be more neutral or technical (e.g., 'Re: New Sequences Window').

value_patterns: Contains email headers, URLs, special characters, and line breaks
May include HTML-like tags or encoded characters
Includes natural language text with punctuation and formatting
Length varies widely, from short messages to very long emails

constraints.format_pattern: Free text email body with possible embedded URLs, headers, and encoded characters

body.generation_instructions: Generate multi-sentence paragraphs resembling email bodies. Include realistic email formatting such as headers (Date, From, Message-ID), URLs, line breaks, and occasional encoded or special characters. Malicious bodies often contain promotional content, offers, or calls to action; benign bodies are more conversational or technical.
body.relationship_to_label: Malicious bodies frequently contain marketing language, discount offers, or suspicious links. Benign bodies are more likely to contain technical discussions, replies, or neutral content.

label.generation_instructions: Assign label 1 for malicious samples and 0 for benign samples exactly as per original encoding.
label.relationship_to_label: Target variable indicating malicious (1) or benign (0) email.

value_patterns: Limited set of unique values (5 unique)

allowed_values: Other possible source values as per original dataset

source.generation_instructions: Randomly assign one of the original source categories, preserving the original distribution if known. Use exact string values as in the original data.
source.relationship_to_label: Source may correlate with label distribution; some sources may have higher malicious content.

value_generation_strategy.malicious_samples: Generate 'subject' and 'body' text with promotional, urgent, or marketing language patterns. Include URLs, special characters, and formatting typical of spam/phishing emails. Assign label=1 and sample 'source' from categories associated with malicious data.
value_generation_strategy.benign_samples: Generate 'subject' and 'body' text with neutral, technical, or conversational language. Include email headers and typical mailing list or reply formatting. Assign label=0 and sample 'source' from categories associated with benign data.

quality_checks: Verify column names and order exactly match ['subject', 'body', 'label', 'source']
Ensure data types match: 'subject' and 'body' as object (string), 'label' as int64 with values 0 or 1, 'source' as object with allowed categories
Check no unexpected nulls beyond original counts (subject nulls ≤ 753, body nulls ≤ 1, label and source no nulls)
Validate label encoding strictly limited to 0 and 1
Confirm 'source' values are only from original set of 5 unique strings
Ensure generated text fields follow length and pattern distributions similar to original samples
Maintain approximate label distribution ratio (~51% malicious, ~49% benign)
Cross-check correlations: promotional language in 'subject' and 'body' aligns with label=1, neutral language aligns with label=0
